blocks.text: 1. Bi-Encoder
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447444914-595721148.png
Bi-Encoder revisits a model already introduced back in Dense Retrieval: the faster, more scalable alternative used earlier in the pipeline.
It embeds the query and each chunk separately, then compares the resulting vectors, the scalable counterpart to the cross encoder.
2. The Already Familiar Model
Dense Retrieval already used a bi-encoder to embed queries and chunks independently.
This topic revisits that same architecture, now explicitly contrasted against the cross encoder.
3. Separate Encoding Paths
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447444914-523184002.png
As with processing both together in Cross Encoder, a cross encoder combined query and chunk into one input.
A bi-encoder instead runs two completely separate encoding passes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model type","Encoding structure"],"rows":[["Cross encoder","One combined pass over query and chunk together"],["Bi-encoder","Two separate passes, one for query, one for chunk"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Why Precomputing Changes Everything
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447444915-888511299.png
As with no caching possible in Cross Encoder, a cross encoder can never precompute anything ahead of time.
A bi-encoder's separate paths mean chunk embeddings can be computed once and reused forever.
5. Comparing Vectors After Encoding
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447445128-622606751.png
As with similarity metrics covered in Similarity Metrics, once both vectors exist, a fast similarity calculation produces the final score.
That comparison step is dramatically cheaper than a full cross encoder pass.
6. Scaling To Millions Of Candidates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447445129-314933321.png
As with computational cost per candidate in Cross Encoder, a bi-encoder can score millions of precomputed vectors in the time a cross encoder scores a handful.
This makes bi-encoders the only realistic choice for first stage retrieval at scale.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Scoring one million precomputed chunk vectors against a single query embedding takes a fraction of a second with a bi-encoder, while a cross encoder running that same volume would take dramatically longer.

blocks.text: 7. The Accuracy Tradeoff Revisited
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447445129-441811650.png
As with the accuracy versus scalability tradeoff in Cross Encoder, a bi-encoder sacrifices some of the precision a cross encoder achieves.
That gap is exactly what re-ranking with a cross encoder afterward exists to close.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: The precision lost by a bi-encoder's separate encoding paths is exactly why a two stage pipeline pairs it with a cross encoder afterward, recovering that accuracy on just the narrowed candidate set.

blocks.text: 8. Both Encoder Types In One Pipeline
As with where cross encoders actually run in Cross Encoder, a real pipeline uses a bi-encoder first, then a cross encoder second.
Each encoder type does the job it is actually best suited for.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When A Bi-Encoder Is The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Recognizing When A Bi-Encoder Is The Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447445129-141981366.png
First stage retrieval across large collections needs a bi-encoder.
Final, precise ranking of a small candidate set needs a cross encoder instead, as covered in Cross Encoder.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates precomputing chunk embeddings once and comparing them against a fresh query embedding.

code.content:
import time

def fake_embed(text):
    # Separate encoding path: embed text independently
    words = text.lower().split()
    return (len(words), sum(len(w) for w in words))

def cosine_like_similarity(v1, v2):
    dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v1, v2))
    mag1 = sum(a * a for a in v1) ** 0.5
    mag2 = sum(a * a for a in v2) ** 0.5
    return dot / (mag1 * mag2) if mag1 and mag2 else 0

chunks = [
    "Refunds are processed within five business days.",
    "Shipping timelines vary by region.",
    "Damaged items qualify for a full refund.",
]

print("Precomputing chunk embeddings once:")
start = time.time()
chunk_embeddings = [fake_embed(c) for c in chunks]
print(f"  Precompute time: {time.time() - start:.5f} seconds\n")

query = "how long does a refund take"
query_embedding = fake_embed(query)

print("Comparing the fresh query embedding against precomputed chunk vectors:")
for chunk, emb in zip(chunks, chunk_embeddings):
    score = cosine_like_similarity(query_embedding, emb)
    print(f"  {score:.3f}: {chunk!r}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows chunk embeddings computed once upfront, with only a fast similarity comparison needed at query time.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a bi-encoder alone when maximum final ranking accuracy matters most.
Recomputing chunk embeddings on every query instead of precomputing and reusing them.
Assuming a bi-encoder matches a cross encoder's accuracy without accounting for the tradeoff.
Skipping a bi-encoder entirely and using only a cross encoder, which cannot scale to large collections.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each chunk separately, then compares the resulting vectors.
It is the same architecture already introduced generally in Dense Retrieval.
Unlike a cross encoder, it runs two completely separate encoding passes.
Its separate paths mean chunk embeddings can be computed once and reused forever.
A fast similarity calculation compares the vectors, far cheaper than a full cross encoder pass.
A bi-encoder can score millions of precomputed vectors in the time a cross encoder scores a handful.
It sacrifices some precision compared to a cross encoder, which re-ranking recovers afterward.
A real pipeline uses a bi-encoder first for retrieval, then a cross encoder second for re-ranking.
